[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Introduction to Blockchain Tables in Oracle Database"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Blockchain tables in Oracle Database provide an immutable and tamper-evident data storage solution. They are designed to prevent unauthorized modifications and deletions of data, making them suitable for applications requiring high levels of data integrity and auditability. This tutorial will guide you through the key concepts and practical steps for creating and using blockchain tables."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Key Concepts"},{"order":4,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Immutability: Once data is inserted into a blockchain table, it cannot be modified or deleted directly. Updates are handled by inserting new rows with the updated information."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Chain Data: Each row in a blockchain table contains a hash of the previous row, creating a chain of data that ensures data integrity. Any attempt to tamper with the data will break the chain and be easily detectable."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"User Authorization: Access to blockchain tables can be controlled through standard Oracle Database security mechanisms, such as roles and privileges."},{"order":7,"type":"subheading","text":"Creating a Blockchain Table"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"To create a blockchain table, you use the 'CREATE TABLE' statement with the 'BLOCKCHAIN' clause. Here's a basic example:"},{"order":9,"type":"code","text":"CREATE TABLE transaction_history (
  transaction_id NUMBER PRIMARY KEY,
  account_id NUMBER,
  amount NUMBER,
  transaction_date DATE
) BLOCKCHAIN;"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"This statement creates a blockchain table named 'transaction_history' with four columns: 'transaction_id', 'account_id', 'amount', and 'transaction_date'. The 'BLOCKCHAIN' clause specifies that this is a blockchain table."},{"order":11,"type":"subheading","text":"Advanced Blockchain Table Options"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"You can customize the behavior of blockchain tables using additional options in the 'BLOCKCHAIN' clause. Some important options include:"},{"order":13,"type":"bullet_point","text":"NO DROP UNTIL integer DAYS: Prevents the table from being dropped for a specified number of days after the last row was inserted. For example, 'NO DROP UNTIL 30 DAYS'."},{"order":14,"type":"bullet_point","text":"NO DELETE UNTIL integer DAYS: Prevents rows from being deleted for a specified number of days after they were inserted. For example, 'NO DELETE UNTIL 90 DAYS'."},{"order":15,"type":"bullet_point","text":"HASHING USING algorithm: Specifies the hashing algorithm to use for calculating the row hash. The default is 'SHA2_512'. For example, 'HASHING USING SHA2_512'."},{"order":16,"type":"code","text":"CREATE TABLE transaction_history (
  transaction_id NUMBER PRIMARY KEY,
  account_id NUMBER,
  amount NUMBER,
  transaction_date DATE
) BLOCKCHAIN
NO DROP UNTIL 30 DAYS
NO DELETE UNTIL 90 DAYS
HASHING USING SHA2_512;"},{"order":17,"type":"subheading","text":"Inserting Data into a Blockchain Table"},{"order":18,"type":"paragraph","text":"Inserting data into a blockchain table is similar to inserting data into a regular table. Use the 'INSERT' statement:"},{"order":19,"type":"code","text":"INSERT INTO transaction_history (transaction_id, account_id, amount, transaction_date)
VALUES (1, 101, 100.00, SYSDATE);"},{"order":20,"type":"subheading","text":"Updating Data in a Blockchain Table"},{"order":21,"type":"paragraph","text":"Since blockchain tables are immutable, you cannot directly update existing rows. Instead, you insert a new row with the updated information. You might want to include a version number or effective date to track changes."},{"order":22,"type":"code","text":"INSERT INTO transaction_history (transaction_id, account_id, amount, transaction_date)
VALUES (1, 101, 120.00, SYSDATE);"},{"order":23,"type":"paragraph","text":"In this example, we insert a new row with the same 'transaction_id' but an updated 'amount'. You would typically query the table to retrieve the latest version of the data."},{"order":24,"type":"subheading","text":"Querying Data from a Blockchain Table"},{"order":25,"type":"paragraph","text":"Querying data from a blockchain table is the same as querying data from a regular table. You can use 'SELECT' statements with various 'WHERE' clauses to retrieve the desired information."},{"order":26,"type":"code","text":"SELECT * FROM transaction_history
WHERE account_id = 101;"},{"order":27,"type":"subheading","text":"Verifying Data Integrity"},{"order":28,"type":"paragraph","text":"Oracle provides functions to verify the integrity of the blockchain. You can use the 'DBMS_BLOCKCHAIN_TABLE' package to validate the chain and detect any tampering."},{"order":29,"type":"code","text":"SELECT DBMS_BLOCKCHAIN_TABLE.verify_table('transaction_history') FROM dual;"},{"order":30,"type":"paragraph","text":"This query will return 'TRUE' if the blockchain is intact and 'FALSE' if any tampering is detected."},{"order":31,"type":"subheading","text":"Conclusion"},{"order":32,"type":"paragraph","text":"Blockchain tables in Oracle Database offer a powerful way to ensure data integrity and prevent unauthorized modifications. By understanding the key concepts and following the steps outlined in this tutorial, you can effectively use blockchain tables in your applications to enhance data security and auditability."}]
